Patients with sulfonamide allergy
Sulfonamide allergy is the contraindication to sulfacetamide among the ocular antibiotics, and has nothing to do with alpha agonists.
Patients over 65, because of falls
Age over 65 is not a contraindication. The age limit runs the other way — under two years.
Children under two, from apnoea risk
Correct. A hard age contraindication, and the mechanism is the same central alpha-2 effect that makes imidazoline ingestion dangerous in toddlers. Worth holding alongside that question.

glauc2.io: Identify indications and contraindications of ophthalmic drugs
glauc2.q: A patient using latanoprost thinks two drops a night will lower the pressure further. What should they be told?
opts: Two drops a night is acceptable if the pressure is not at target
It would work against the goal rather than toward it: exceeding once daily actively inhibits the pressure-lowering effect.
It is harmless but wasteful
Not harmless. The extra dose is not merely wasted; it reduces the pressure-lowering effect the patient is taking the drug for.
It should be split to morning and evening instead
Splitting the dose still exceeds once daily in total, so the same inhibition of the pressure-lowering effect applies.
Exceeding once daily dosing inhibits the pressure-lowering effect
Correct. This is counter-intuitive and therefore a good question: more drug does not mean more effect, it means less. Once daily is the maximum as well as the minimum.

glauc2.io: Describe the mechanism of action of ophthalmic drugs
glauc2.q: How do dorzolamide and brinzolamide lower pressure?
opts: They increase outflow through the trabecular meshwork
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors do not act on drainage at all; they reduce bicarbonate production so less fluid is made.
They block beta receptors in the ciliary body
That is the beta blockers, though both end up reducing production.
They inhibit carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary epithelium
Correct. Less bicarbonate means less fluid follows it, so aqueous production falls. It is a production-side drug, like the beta blockers but by a different route.
They activate muscarinic receptors on the ciliary muscle
That is the cholinergic agonists, which contract the ciliary muscle and open the trabecular meshwork to increase outflow.

glauc2.io: Describe the mechanism of action of ophthalmic drugs
glauc2.q: Glaucoma drugs work by one of two strategies. What are they?
opts: Decreasing aqueous production or reducing episcleral venous pressure
Episcleral venous pressure is not one of the two targets; drug therapy works on production and on outflow.
Increasing outflow or reducing optic nerve metabolic demand
Neuroprotection is not among the described mechanisms; the drugs are pressure drugs.
Dilating the pupil or constricting the ciliary muscle
Cholinergics do contract the ciliary muscle, but as a means to increase outflow rather than as a strategy in itself.
Reducing production or increasing outflow
Correct. Every agent in this section sorts into one or the other, and some do both. Sorting a drug by which side it is on is the fastest way to remember the whole class list.

glauc2.io: Identify indications and contraindications of ophthalmic drugs
glauc2.q: Which patients with raised pressure are treated, and which are monitored?
opts: Treat those with risk factors; monitor those without
Correct. Raised pressure alone is not automatically a prescription. Risk factors decide, and in their absence you watch for the change that would make it a disease.
All patients with pressure above 21 mmHg are treated
That would treat every ocular hypertensive, which is not the stated approach.
Only those who already have visual field loss are treated
Waiting for field loss means waiting for irreversible axon loss, which is what treatment exists to prevent.
Treatment is started only once both eyes are affected
Not a criterion given, and therapy may deliberately start in one eye.

glauc2.io: Identify indications and contraindications of ophthalmic drugs
glauc2.q: For which procedures are topical ocular anaesthetics indicated?
opts: Fundoscopy and pupil assessment
Those need dilation, which is what the cycloplegics and phenylephrine are for.
Treatment of corneal abrasion pain at home
Explicitly ruled out: these are not prescribed for home use, because repeated application is toxic to the epithelium and delays healing.
Tonometry, foreign body removal, corneal surgery
Correct. All three need the surface insensate but not the eye immobilised. That also explains why tonometry cannot simply be done on any patient without preparation.
Intravitreal injection only
Not the listed indications, which are all anterior and superficial.

glauc2.io: Identify indications and contraindications of ophthalmic drugs
opts: Prostaglandins, beta blockers and cholinergic agonists
Prostaglandins and cholinergic agonists are outflow drugs, so neither belongs on a list of agents that reduce aqueous production.
Alpha agonists, beta blockers and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
Correct. The alpha agonists sit on both sides of the list, which is the part most easily got wrong — they reduce production AND increase outflow.
Cholinergic agonists and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors only
Cholinergics work on outflow by contracting the ciliary muscle.
Prostaglandins alone
Prostaglandins are the first-line agents but they work by increasing outflow, which puts them on the other side of this division.

glauc2.io: Describe the mechanism of action of ophthalmic drugs
glauc2.q: How do atropine, cyclopentolate and tropicamide produce mydriasis?
opts: They competitively block muscarinic acetylcholine receptors

Correct. Blocking muscarinic receptors is the exact opposite of pilocarpine's action, which is why one dilates and the other constricts. They are used diagnostically and in uveitis to prevent synechiae and relieve ciliary spasm.
They activate alpha-1 adrenergic receptors
That is phenylephrine, the sympathomimetic route to the same endpoint.
They activate muscarinic receptors on the iris dilator
Activating muscarinic receptors constricts the pupil, as pilocarpine does. Dilation requires blocking them, not stimulating them.
They inhibit carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary body
Carbonic anhydrase inhibition is a glaucoma mechanism that lowers pressure and has no effect on pupil size at all.

glauc2.io: Describe the mechanism of action of ophthalmic drugs
glauc2.q: How do ophthalmic alpha-2 agonists lower intraocular pressure?
opts: They block beta receptors in the ciliary epithelium
That is the beta blockers, which reduce production by cutting cyclic AMP in the ciliary epithelium rather than improving drainage.
They reduce production and increase outflow
Correct. They work on both sides of the equation, which is why they appear in both lists — decreased production and increased outflow.
They contract the ciliary muscle to open the trabecular meshwork
That is the cholinergic agonists, which contract the ciliary muscle and open the trabecular meshwork to increase outflow.
They analogue prostaglandin F2-alpha at prostaglandin receptors
That is the prostaglandin analogues, which bind prostaglandin receptors and increase outflow as the first-line agents.

glauc2.io: Describe the mechanism of action of ophthalmic drugs
glauc2.q: How do ophthalmic beta blockers lower intraocular pressure?
opts: They block beta receptors in the ciliary epithelium
Correct. Less catecholamine activation means less cyclic AMP, and less aqueous is made. They act on the production side, not on drainage.
They increase outflow through the trabecular meshwork
Increasing outflow is what the prostaglandins and the cholinergic agonists do; the beta blockers work on production instead.
They inhibit carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary epithelium
A different production-side mechanism belonging to dorzolamide and brinzolamide.
They contract the ciliary muscle
That is the cholinergic agonists, and it opens outflow rather than reducing production.

glauc2.io: Identify indications and contraindications of ophthalmic drugs
glauc2.q: What is the general target for pressure reduction in glaucoma therapy?
opts: A pressure below 10 mmHg in every patient
Below 10 is under the normal range; the target is relative, not a universal floor.
A 50 per cent reduction regardless of starting pressure
More aggressive than the stated goal, and it would mean more drugs and more side effects.
Any reduction at all, however small
Any reduction at all is too permissive to count as a target; the stated goal is a 20 to 30 per cent fall in pressure.
A 20 to 30 per cent reduction in intraocular pressure
Correct. The goal is expressed as a proportion rather than an absolute number, which matches the stated aim: prevent progressive optic nerve damage with the least risk and fewest side effects.

glauc2.io: Identify indications and contraindications of ophthalmic drugs
glauc2.q: Which classes are named as reasonable places to START glaucoma therapy?
opts: A carbonic anhydrase inhibitor or a cholinergic agonist
Both are available, but neither is offered as the usual starting point — tolerability is the problem with each.
A prostaglandin analogue or a beta blocker
Correct. Either is a reasonable opening move, though the prostaglandins are described as first line and the most commonly used, with beta blockers second line.
A combination product from the outset
Combinations are for when multiple agents are needed, not for starting.
A cholinergic agonist alone
Compliance is poor because of side effects and frequent dosing, so it is a poor first choice.
